CLS's statement of faith would exclude from participation any student who engages in same-sex conduct and any student who holds different religious convictions than those established in the statement of faith. Id.
``[Christian Legal Society (CLS)], it bears emphasis,
seeks not parity with other organizations, but a
preferential exemption from Hastings' policy. The First
Amendment shields CLS against state prohibition of the
organization's expressive activity, however
exclusionary that activity may be. But CLS enjoys no
constitutional right to state subvention of its
selectivity.''\20\
\20\Id. at 669.
Though CLS refused to alter its policies to open its organization to all students to gain official recognition, Hastings Law School nonetheless offered CLS access to its facilities for meetings and activities.\21\ The Court noted that ``Hastings . . . is dangling the carrot of subsidy, not wielding the stick of prohibition'' in its implementing the all-comers policy for its official student organizations, which receive access to funding.\22\ In other words, Hastings was not barring CLS from campus for its choice to discriminate, it merely prevented it from becoming an official student group which receives funding paid for with fees collected from all students because it chose to discriminate. CLS could reverse course and welcome all students if it chose and receive funding.
\21\Id. at 673.
\22\Id. at 683.
H.R. 5505 would place the First Amendment rights of religious organizations above all other rights, as it could provide exemptions for religious student organizations when their practices conflict with the rules established for all other student organizations. In the end, students will be harmed. In fact, H.R. 5505 would in some cases require students--who must pay activity fees to fund student clubs-- subsidize groups that discriminate against them. As a result, H.R. 5505 would interfere with institutional policies that are permissible under the First Amendment and designed to maximize participation in officially recognized student organizations.\23\
\23\However, the First Amendment requires public IHEs to administer its policies for student organizations in an even-handed manner. Several recent lower court cases have affirmed religious student organizations' challenge to nondiscrimination policies due to the schools' uneven enforcement of its own nondiscrimination policies. See, e.g., InterVarsity Christian Fellowship v. Wayne State University, The Becket Fund for Religious Liberty, https://becketfund.org/case/ intervarsity-christian-fellowship-v-wayne-state-university/ (last accessed July 30, 2026).
H.R. 5505 goes further than the 2020 Trump Administration Regulation
Supporters of H.R. 5505 claim that the legislation is intended to codify a regulation put in place by the first Trump Administration.\24\ In 2020, the Department finalized a rule (2020 Final Rule) to prohibit public IHEs from denying a religious student organization any benefits that are otherwise afforded to other student organizations because of the organization's ``beliefs, practices, policies, speech, membership standards, or leadership standards, which are informed by sincerely held religious beliefs.''\25\ The 2020 Final Rule applies to several grant programs under HEA, but it does not apply to funding associated with student financial aid.\26\ In contrast, H.R. 5505 applies to the entirety of funding for Title IV student financial aid.
\24\Press Release, Rep. Tim Walberg, Walberg, Lankford, Scott Introduce Equal Campus Access Act (Sept. 18, 2025), https:// walberg.house.gov/media/press-releases/walberg-lankford-scott-introduce-equal-campus-access-act.
\25\Direct Grant Programs, State Administered Formula Grant Programs, Non Discrimination on the Basis of Sex in Education Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance, Developing Hispanic Serving Institutions Program, Strengthening Institutions Program, Strengthening Historically Black Colleges and Universities Program, and Strengthening Historically Black Graduate Institutions Program, 85 Fed. Reg. 59916, 59943 (Sept. 23, 2020) (codified at 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d) and 34 C.F.R. 76.500(d) (hereinafter 2020 Final Rule).
\26\Id. at 59924.
Furthermore, the preamble to the 2020 Final Rule states that public institutions may still adopt ``all-comers'' policies under the rule, as long as religious student organizations are not treated any differently than other student organizations.''\27\ H.R. 5505 fails to provide the assurance found in the 2020 Final Rule, that all-comer policies would be permissible.\28\ It should be noted, however, there is nothing in the plain regulatory text\29\ in the 2020 Final Rule that could be read to allow IHEs to adopt all-comer policies and still be in compliance.\30\ As a result, H.R. 5505 will only add to the confusion for public IHEs in terms of what policies they will be able to apply to their official student organizations. Lost in this debate are the students who could be denied opportunities to join and seek leadership positions in officially recognized organizations that are funded by them with their mandatory student activity fees.
\27\Id. at 59966.
\28\In 2023, the Biden Administration proposed rescinding the 2020 Final Rule, reasoning, in part, that the 2020 Final Rule created confusion because it could be construed to require IHEs to afford preferential treatment and prohibit IHEs from applying neutral and generally applicable nondiscrimination policies. See Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Program, 88 Fed. Reg. 10857 (Feb. 22, 2023) (proposed rescission of 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d) and 76.500(d)) (hereinafter Proposed 2020 Recission). On December 26, 2024, the Biden Administration withdrew the proposal to rescind the regulation citing in part to the upcoming change in administration. See Direct Grant Programs, State-Administered Formula Grant Programs; Withdrawal, 89 Fed. Reg. 104935 (Dec. 26, 2024) (withdrawal of proposed rescission of 34 C.F.R. Sec. Sec. 75.500(d) and 76.500(d)) (hereinafter 2020 Recission Withdrawal).
\29\See 34 C.F.R. Sec. 75.500(d); 34 C.F.R. Sec. 76.500(d).
\30\Proposed 2020 Recission, supra note 28, at 10860 (``There is nothing in the regulatory text that clarifies or guarantees that an institution may insist that such religious organizations comply with the same neutral and generally-applicable practices, policies, and membership and leadership standards that apply equally to nonreligious student organizations, including but not limited to nondiscrimination requirements.'').
In the end, H.R. 5505 would have the effect of codifying the 2020 Final Rule with a broader application to the entirety of HEA, including Title IV student financial aid. As a result, H.R. 5505 would enshrine in law a policy to give religious student organizations preferential treatment, exempting religious student clubs from nondiscrimination and potentially other requirements that apply to all other officially recognized student organizations.
DEMOCRATIC AMENDMENTS OFFERED DURING MARKUP OF H.R. 5505
Committee Democrats put forward two amendments. The amendment offered by Rep. Lucy McBath (D-GA) would have ensured that public IHEs may deny privileges to student organizations, including religious student organizations, that violate institutional policies related to nondiscrimination and anti-hazing. The second amendment offered by Rep. Suzanne Bonamici (D-OR) prohibited the use of interagency agreements related to enforcement of requirements for campus access for religious student organizations and requires the Secretary of Education to carry out enforcement of the provisions of H.R. 5505, as it amends HEA. Both amendments failed on party lines.

CONCLUSION
For the reasons stated above, all Committee Democrats present unanimously opposed H.R. 5505 when the Committee on Education and Workforce considered it on June 25, 2026. We urge the House of Representatives to do the same.
Robert C. ``Bobby'' Scott,
